text: Today we are introducing our second model generation with Inkling 2 Small. It is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters, 17B active, and supports image inputs and variable effort. Inkling 2 Small far surpasses our previous models’ scores on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 31, reflecting gains in performance on agentic coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning. The increase in capabilities comes from improvements made at every step of our training process, including more efficient pre-training and a large, unified RL run. Inkling 2 Small will initially be available through Tinker, with closed weights, following the approach we outlined in a safe path to open weights . We intend to make the full weights available under an Apache 2.0 license next week after the completion of external safety testing and red-teaming. You can try Inkling 2 Small on Tinker Playground today. The model is also available for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker; checkpoints will be downloadable with the release of Inkling 2 Small’s weights. Inkling 2 Small is more capable across the board than our first generation, particularly in long-horizon autonomous work. Inkling 2 Small’s vision and agentic capabilities enable it to incorporate visual feedback to iteratively build and refine websites, games, and 3D designs with interactive elements. Inkling 2 Small was trained with RL on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks across multiple agent harnesses and context-compaction strategies. We increased the quality of our synthetic coding data pipeline and moved beyond unit-test rewards alone; many tasks included an agentic RL grader that evaluated how the model approached the problem, not just whether its code passed. We also tested early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small on OpenCode under the name Fledge-Alpha to assess our model’s performance on coding tasks in the real world. The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops. Inkling 2 Small improves on usability compared to Inkling: it follows instructions better, considers changes carefully, and verifies its work without being asked. Beyond conventional software tasks, Inkling 2 Small was also trained on long-horizon autoresearch tasks. This included agentic GPU kernel optimization and ML tasks such as post-training a model autonomously, all run across a range of GPU architectures. Inkling 2 Small autonomously trained Qwen3.5-4B on Tinker to predict various time series such as weather and Wikipedia page views. It started by analyzing the tasks and writing its own evaluator, experimented with training datasets and recipes, and tried various approaches to SFT and RL, while debugging the process as it goes. After 4.5 hours of work and $426 in Tinker spend, the trained model has more than doubled its forecasting score. Inkling 2 Small processes image inputs using a 292M-parameter vision encoder based on Perception Encoder Bolya et al., 2025 . . We use 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling, and interleave image patches with text tokens. The model demonstrates strong visual capabilities across multiple categories, including OCR, grounding, infographic interpretation, and visual reasoning. The model uses vision in the loop to interpret and validate the visual coding output it generates. Pending the release of its weights, it is set to be the top open-weights model on DesignArena . DesignArena Website score We even tested Inkling 2 Small against some of our researchers in a wine tasting event. It outperformed them using vision alone, correctly identifying three wines from a single picture in 19 out of 20 trials. Prompt: you’re in a blind wine tasting competition. glasses are labeled 1 to 3 from left to right. varietals: 99 cab sauv, 19 cab sauv, 23 nebbiolo Inkling 2 Small: Here’s my read — with the big caveat up front that color from a phone photo under warm restaurant lighting is shaky evidence, so treat this as an educated guess, not a verdict. My guess: Glass 1 = 2019 Cabernet Sauvignon Glass 2 = 1999 Cabernet Sauvignon Glass 3 = 2023 Nebbiolo Why: The honest weak points in that guess: lighting is uneven (the left glass sits in the dimmer zone near the hearth, which exaggerates its darkness), and a well-stored 1999 can drink much darker than it looks on camera. Hue differences, not depth, would be the real tell — if glass 2 shows orange/brown at the rim versus glass 1’s purple-red edge, that confirms it. Fast sensory tie-breakers when you actually taste: If the pour in glass 3 is pale but your mouth feels sanded down by tannins, that’s the slam-dunk nebbiolo confirmation; if it is soft and plush, flip glass 3 and glass 2. Good luck in the competition — report back with the reveal if you get it. Inkling 2 Small accelerates knowledge work in realistic professional environments. It proficiently looks up information, calls tools over MCP, and produces high-quality deliverables. On AA-Briefcase, an end-to-end knowledge work benchmark, these capabilities come together for an ELO score of 1527. Inkling 2 Small is especially strong in finance and quantitative reasoning over spreadsheets, filings and documents. Among open weight models, Inkling 2 Small is the best performing model across several finance benchmarks. Some models respond better to fine-tuning, independent of their out-of-the-box performance. We wanted Inkling 2 Small to be a strong base model for customization. Inkling 2 Small learns faster and improves more than our previous models when trained on the same data and algorithm across a variety of post-training scenarios, which we curated based on customer use cases. For example, starting from similarly low scores on a public financial-document summarization task, Inkling 2 Small adapts quickly, reaching the final performance of Inkling Small with just 75 training steps and finishing substantially ahead. Evaluating Model Finetunability Inkling 2 Small is trained on challenging STEM problems, instruction following, information seeking with and without web search, and forecasting tasks. During RL, we use proper scoring rules for forecasting tasks and uncertainty-sensitive rewards on some question-answering tasks. This trained the model to assess uncertainty, express appropriate confidence, and make well-calibrated predictions. Our safety work for Inkling 2 Small centers on two questions: how the model performs for the general user, and how well it resists the removal of safeguards by a malicious actor. The release of Inkling’s weights is pending further safety evaluations by us and our partners. To assess misuse risks, we trained an internal helpful-only variant. We ran both this model and the release checkpoint through a wider suite of evaluations, with more external testers, than any previous release. On chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risk, Inkling 2 Small’s knowledge and capability scores sit below the open-weight frontier. On FORTRESS, Scale AI’s private benchmark that scores how much harmful assistance a model gives in response to expert-written adversarial prompts across CBRN, terrorism, and nonviolent crime, Inkling 2 Small has a lower Average Risk Score compared with Inkling and Inkling-Small, and also demonstrates a higher Overrefusal Score (see Limitations). The helpful-only variant of Inkling 2 Small exhibits marginal uplift on CBRN knowledge relative to the release checkpoint, but it does not significantly advance the frontier on any dimension we measured. On offensive and dual-use agentic cyber benchmarks, Inkling 2 Small is a large step up from Inkling Small but remains behind the open-weight frontier. It matches the open-weight frontier on Vals CyberBench v1.1 and PatchEval, both of which measure the ability to find and patch security vulnerabilities. * While we handle mental distress situations well, our model sometimes overreacts with disclaimers in normal emotional support queries as mentioned in the Limitations section. As models take on unsupervised, longer-horizon autonomous work, the potential harm from their misbehavior increases. Without proper attention to alignment, capabilities-focused RL can push models to succeed at any cost. When tasks were difficult, early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small were persistent in trying to succeed—in some cases fabricating results, ignoring instructions, and concealing what they had done. We worked across the stack to improve model alignment. In midtraining, we filtered out traces containing misbehavior and included traces with honest, aligned behavior. In RL, we added a general alignment reward that penalizes misbehavior on every task. We also built environments targeting specific failure modes we observed in training, such as rewarding models for giving up on impossible tasks. Finally, we used on-policy self-distillation Zhao et al., 2026 . from a teacher model prompted with a conduct spec, so the model internalizes principles for good behavior without explicit prompting. We measured progress with both internal and external evaluations, and found that Inkling 2 Small substantially improves over previous Inkling models on both internal and external evaluations, and outperforms a set of comparable open-weights models on our internal evals. Inkling 2 Small still trails closed-weights models, such as GPT-6.1 Sol on our alignment evaluations. Reducing this gap is a priority for future models. We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory. Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon. Internal Code Cutoff 2026-06 · Bits per byte (lower is better) We followed this initial phase with a second phase (H2) of 3.8 trillion tokens of higher-quality, newer data the model hadn’t seen, at 512K context. The third and fourth phases mixed in data in the deployment format. The third phase was about 320 billion tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context, alongside replayed pretraining data. The fourth phase (H4) kept only the highest-quality data: about 34 billion tokens of agent trajectories. The H3 and H4 mixtures consisted mostly of trajectories sampled from earlier models including Kimi K3 and our own models, filtered for correctness and alignment. We then carried out a joint RL run, consisting of 1,075 steps and over 17 million rollouts over 9 days. See table below for more details. This single joint run contrasts with the previous Inkling release, where we ran separate reasoning and agentic RL runs and combined them with multi-teacher distillation. The task mix included software engineering in real repositories, terminal tasks, document creation, STEM question answering, vision, web app building, tool use with simulated users, and safety. Each task family had its own grader: hidden unit tests and programmatic checks for most coding work; rubric-based LLM judges for documents and tool use; reference answers for STEM and vision question answering; pairwise reward models comparing screenshots of rendered web apps. We randomly sampled and conditioned on an effort level, and applied a length penalty in the reward function, which trained the model to trade off speed and thoroughness. Our asynchronous RL uses a score centering variant—the StableReinforce objective in Tinker—which tolerates significant staleness. Our run combines short and long horizon tasks with p50/p99 total rollout tokens being 43k and 1.5M respectively and p50/p99 duration of 8 minutes and 4 hours respectively. We use 256k context length and enable compaction training for long-horizon tasks. As a result, both training reward and evaluation performance grow log-linearly with compute. Training reward Mean reward STEM evaluation performance STEM evaluation score Vision evaluation performance Vision evaluation score Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals. Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above. Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon. Like previous Inkling releases, we benchmarked Inkling-Small on a broad range of capabilities. All evals run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. All evals run with a 1M-token maximum trajectory limit, increased from the 256K-token limit used for Inkling Small. While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills. Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio. Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries. We are proud to make Inkling 2 Small available on Tinker for inference and fine tuning. Following the completion of safety testing, the model will be available on additional platforms in the coming weeks. Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. We hope that it encourages your ambitions, and we look forward to seeing what you build with it.
